Section 6 • \(P\)3D with the discrete Fourier transform

6.3 Relation to the per-sample 2PCF: circular correlation and wrap-around

Expanding the product in Eq. (6.5) and grouping the pairs of cells by their lag \((\vec{l},m')\), using that \(e^{2\pi i\vec{p}\cdot\vec{n}/N_\perp}\) and \(e^{2\pi iqm/N_\Lambda}\) are periodic on the grid, gives the discrete Wiener–Khinchin theorem, exact for every realization: \begin{align} \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[\vec{p},q] &= v\sum_{\vec{l}}\sum_{m'=0}^{N_\Lambda-1} \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s),\circlearrowleft}[\vec{l},m']\; e^{+2\pi i\left(\vec{p}\cdot\vec{l}/N_\perp+q\,m'/N_\Lambda\right)}, \notag\\ \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s),\circlearrowleft}[\vec{l},m'] &\equiv \frac{1}{N}\sum_{\vec{n}}\sum_{m} \delta_i^{(s)}[\vec{n},m]\, \delta_j^{(s)}[\vec{n}+\vec{l},m+m'], \tag{6.6} \end{align} with the indices of the second field taken modulo the grid. \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s),\circlearrowleft}\) is the circular 2PCF: every cell has a partner at every lag, at the price of wrapping around the edges (Fig. 13).

Periodic domain.

For a simulation box the fields are genuinely periodic, the wrapped pairs are physical pairs, and \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s),\circlearrowleft}\) is the discrete version of Eq. (4.2) with periodic boundaries. Eq. (6.6) is then the discrete counterpart of Eq. (5.4) with \(\overline{W}=1\).

Non-periodic domain.

For non-periodic data (e.g. an observed spectrum along the line of sight), the wrapped pairs combine the two ends of the interval. Splitting the sum over \(m\) in Eq. (6.6) into the \(N_\Lambda-m'\) unwrapped pairs, at lag \(m'\), and the \(m'\) wrapped ones, at lag \(m'-N_\Lambda\), \begin{equation} \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s),\circlearrowleft}[m'] = \left(1-\frac{m'}{N_\Lambda}\right)\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}[m'] + \frac{m'}{N_\Lambda}\,\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}[m'-N_\Lambda], \tag{6.7} \end{equation} where \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}[m']\) is the non-periodic estimator of Eq. (4.2) at the lag \(\Delta=m'\,d\Lambda\) (positive or negative); the transverse direction is treated in the same way. Since \(e^{2\pi iq(m'-N_\Lambda)/N_\Lambda}=e^{2\pi iqm'/N_\Lambda}\), inserting this into Eq. (6.6) gives \begin{equation} \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[\vec{p},q] = v\sum_{\vec{l}}\sum_{m'=-(N_\Lambda-1)}^{N_\Lambda-1} \overline{W}[\vec{l},m']\; \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}[\vec{l},m']\; e^{+i\left(\vec{k}_\perp[\vec{p}]\cdot\vec{r}_\perp[\vec{l}]+k_\parallel[q]\,\Delta[m']\right)}, \tag{6.8} \end{equation} with \(\overline{W}[\vec{l},m']\) the discrete version of the window of Eq. (5.4) (\(1-|m'|/N_\Lambda\) along the line of sight): the DFT periodogram is exactly the Riemann sum of Eq. (5.4) at the discrete modes. The wrap-around is therefore not an additional error: it is the same triangular taper of the continuous finite-domain periodogram. Zero-padding the data to \(2N_\Lambda\) cells removes the wrapped pairs from Eq. (6.6), but Eq. (6.8) is unchanged and only evaluated on a finer grid, \(k_{\rm f,\parallel}\to k_{\rm f,\parallel}/2\): padding interpolates the periodogram, it neither removes the window nor adds independent modes.
